Topic 05·Anik Sir · Lectures 5–6

Fourier series

Periodic signals as sums of harmonics, the coefficient formula, symmetry, and the main properties.

3 past questions on this topic

The big idea

Can we break a complicated periodic signal into simple sine and cosine waves? Yes, always (for any reasonable signal).

complicated periodic signal=sum of simple periodic waves.\text{complicated periodic signal}=\text{sum of simple periodic waves}.complicated periodic signal=sum of simple periodic waves.

Why this is useful

  1. Some problems are easy for simple waves: a sine-shaped vibration on a string, or a sinusoidal temperature pattern in a metal rod, evolves in a simple, predictable way.
  2. Real initial shapes are not simple: a string can be plucked into a strange shape, and a rod can start with an arbitrary heat pattern.
  3. Fourier series is the bridge: break the random shape into simple waves, solve each simple wave on its own, then add the answers back together.

This was exactly Fourier's problem: how heat spreads in a solid. The same strategy later powered audio, images, communications and almost all of signal processing.

Which frequencies are allowed?

The bell analogy

Bell A rings every 2 minutes, bell B every 3, bell C every 5. Together the pattern repeats after lcm⁡(2,3,5)=30\operatorname{lcm}(2,3,5)=30lcm(2,3,5)=30 minutes.

Look at the same story in frequency. Periods of 2, 3, 5 minutes are frequencies of 30, 20, 12 rings per hour. The combined pattern repeats every 30 minutes, i.e. at f0=2f_0=2f0​=2 times per hour, and

30=15f0,20=10f0,12=6f0.30=15f_0,\qquad 20=10f_0,\qquad 12=6f_0 .30=15f0​,20=10f0​,12=6f0​.

Every component frequency of a periodic signal is a whole multiple of the signal's own (fundamental) frequency.

Harmonics

A signal with period TTT has fundamental frequency

ω0=2πT.\omega_0=\frac{2\pi}{T}.ω0​=T2π​.

The only building blocks that repeat with period TTT are those at the frequencies kω0k\omega_0kω0​, k∈Zk\in\mathbb Zk∈Z:

…, −2ω0, −ω0, 0, ω0, 2ω0, …\dots,\ -2\omega_0,\ -\omega_0,\ 0,\ \omega_0,\ 2\omega_0,\ \dots…, −2ω0​, −ω0​, 0, ω0​, 2ω0​, …

Complex exponentials instead of sines and cosines

Instead of separate sines and cosines we use complex exponentials, which package both (Euler):

ejω0t=cos⁡ω0t+jsin⁡ω0t.e^{j\omega_0t}=\cos\omega_0t+j\sin\omega_0t .ejω0​t=cosω0​t+jsinω0​t.

Negative kkk rotate backward, positive kkk rotate forward, k=0k=0k=0 is the constant part.

Finding the coefficients

A detour: averaging a rotating exponential

Over one full period, a rotating exponential goes all the way round and its average is 000. A non-rotating constant keeps its value:

1T∫Tejkω0t dt={1,k=00,k≠0\frac1T\int_T e^{jk\omega_0t}\,dt=\begin{cases}1,&k=0\\0,&k\neq0\end{cases}T1​∫T​ejkω0​tdt={1,0,​k=0k=0​

Finding a0a_0a0​: just take the average

x(t)=⋯+a−1e−jω0t+a0+a1ejω0t+a2ej2ω0t+⋯x(t)=\cdots+a_{-1}e^{-j\omega_0t}+a_0+a_1e^{j\omega_0t}+a_2e^{j2\omega_0t}+\cdotsx(t)=⋯+a−1​e−jω0​t+a0​+a1​ejω0​t+a2​ej2ω0​t+⋯

Every term averages to 000 except the constant a0a_0a0​, which survives:

a0=1T∫Tx(t) dt.a_0=\frac1T\int_T x(t)\,dt .a0​=T1​∫T​x(t)dt.

a0a_0a0​ is the average (DC) value of the signal.

Finding a1a_1a1​: make it stop rotating

Multiply the whole series by e−jω0te^{-j\omega_0t}e−jω0​t. Every term's frequency drops by one step:

x(t)e−jω0t=⋯+a−1e−j2ω0t+a0e−jω0t+a1+a2ejω0t+⋯x(t)e^{-j\omega_0t}=\cdots+a_{-1}e^{-j2\omega_0t}+a_0e^{-j\omega_0t}+a_1+a_2e^{j\omega_0t}+\cdotsx(t)e−jω0​t=⋯+a−1​e−j2ω0​t+a0​e−jω0​t+a1​+a2​ejω0​t+⋯

Now a1a_1a1​ is the non-rotating term, so averaging extracts it:

a1=1T∫Tx(t)e−jω0t dt.a_1=\frac1T\int_T x(t)e^{-j\omega_0t}\,dt .a1​=T1​∫T​x(t)e−jω0​tdt.

The general rule

Multiply by e−jkω0te^{-jk\omega_0t}e−jkω0​t to move the wanted coefficient to zero frequency, then average. Everything else keeps rotating and averages away.

 ak=1T∫Tx(t) e−jkω0t dt,k=0,±1,±2,…,ω0=2πT (analysis)\boxed{\,a_k=\frac1T\int_T x(t)\,e^{-jk\omega_0t}\,dt,\qquad k=0,\pm1,\pm2,\dots,\quad\omega_0=\frac{2\pi}{T}\,}\qquad\text{(analysis)}ak​=T1​∫T​x(t)e−jkω0​tdt,k=0,±1,±2,…,ω0​=T2π​​(analysis)

The integral can be taken over any one full period [t0,t0+T][t_0,t_0+T][t0​,t0​+T], since the integrand repeats every TTT.

A beautiful intuition: coordinates

A point in the plane is described by coordinates: (3,2)(3,2)(3,2) means "3 steps along xxx, 2 steps along yyy". Functions can have coordinates too.

  • All functions f(t)=a+btf(t)=a+btf(t)=a+bt have coordinates (a,b)(a,b)(a,b) along the "axes" 111 and ttt. So 3+2t↔(3,2)3+2t\leftrightarrow(3,2)3+2t↔(3,2).
  • With more axes 1,t,t2,t3,…1,t,t^2,t^3,\dots1,t,t2,t3,… we describe more complicated functions: et=1+t+t22!+t33!+⋯e^t=1+t+\frac{t^2}{2!}+\frac{t^3}{3!}+\cdotset=1+t+2!t2​+3!t3​+⋯ has coordinates (1,1,12!,13!,… )\left(1,1,\frac1{2!},\frac1{3!},\dots\right)(1,1,2!1​,3!1​,…).
  • The Fourier series simply chooses different axes: …,e−jω0t,1,ejω0t,ej2ω0t,…\dots,e^{-j\omega_0t},1,e^{j\omega_0t},e^{j2\omega_0t},\dots…,e−jω0​t,1,ejω0​t,ej2ω0​t,…. In these coordinates, cos⁡ω0t\cos\omega_0tcosω0​t has only two non-zero coordinates, 12\frac1221​ at k=±1k=\pm1k=±1.

To find a coordinate of a vector we project: v⋅uv\cdot uv⋅u. For signals, the dot product is an average over one period,

⟨x,z⟩=1T∫Tx(t) z∗(t) dt,\langle x,z\rangle=\frac1T\int_T x(t)\,z^*(t)\,dt,⟨x,z⟩=T1​∫T​x(t)z∗(t)dt,

and projecting onto the kkk-th axis z(t)=ejkω0tz(t)=e^{jk\omega_0t}z(t)=ejkω0​t (so z∗=e−jkω0tz^*=e^{-jk\omega_0t}z∗=e−jkω0​t) gives exactly the coefficient formula. A Fourier coefficient is a projection. Orthogonality of the axes is what makes every other harmonic average to zero.

Convergence: the Dirichlet conditions

The series converges to x(t)x(t)x(t) wherever xxx is continuous, and to the midpoint of each jump, if over one period:

  1. xxx is absolutely integrable: ∫T∣x(t)∣ dt<∞\int_T|x(t)|\,dt<\infty∫T​∣x(t)∣dt<∞;
  2. xxx has a finite number of maxima and minima;
  3. xxx has a finite number of discontinuities, each finite.

Near a jump the partial sums overshoot by about 9%, however many terms are used. This is the Gibbs phenomenon.

Properties of Fourier series

Finding aka_kak​ directly needs an integral. Properties let us reuse a series we already know: shift a signal, scale it, add it, differentiate it, and simply transfer the coefficients. Underneath, every operation on x(t)x(t)x(t) is really an operation on each little wave akejkω0ta_ke^{jk\omega_0t}ak​ejkω0​t.

Throughout, x(t)↔akx(t)\leftrightarrow a_kx(t)↔ak​ and y(t)↔bky(t)\leftrightarrow b_ky(t)↔bk​, both with period TTT.

Linearity

If both signals have the same period, their Fourier axes line up exactly, so the ingredients simply add:

x(t)+y(t)=∑k(ak+bk)ejkω0t⟹Ax(t)+By(t)↔Aak+Bbk.x(t)+y(t)=\sum_k(a_k+b_k)e^{jk\omega_0t}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad Ax(t)+By(t)\leftrightarrow Aa_k+Bb_k .x(t)+y(t)=k∑​(ak​+bk​)ejkω0​t⟹Ax(t)+By(t)↔Aak​+Bbk​.

Time shifting

Does delaying a signal change its frequencies? No. Shift every simple wave underneath:

\end{aligned}$$ Multiplying by $e^{j\phi}$ keeps the radius and rotates the angle by $\phi$. So: - **magnitude unchanged**: $|e^{-jk\omega_0t_0}|=1$; - **phase shifted** by $-k\omega_0t_0$: higher harmonics rotate more, because their frequency is $k\omega_0$. *A delay in time becomes a phase shift in frequency.* Example: $x(t-3)\leftrightarrow a_ke^{-j3k\omega_0}$. ### Time reversal $$\begin{aligned}&x(-t)\\[6pt]&= \sum_ka_ke^{jk\omega_0(-t)}\\[6pt]&= \sum_ka_ke^{j(-k)\omega_0t}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x(-t)\leftrightarrow a_{-k}. \end{aligned}$$ The term that lived at $+k\omega_0$ now lives at $-k\omega_0$: playing the rotation backwards flips its direction. *Reversal in time is index reversal in frequency.* **Problem.** Find the coefficients of $x(4-t)+y(t-3)$. - $x(t+4)\leftrightarrow a_ke^{j4k\omega_0}$ (shift), then reverse: $x(-t+4)\leftrightarrow a_{-k}e^{-j4k\omega_0}$. - $y(t-3)\leftrightarrow b_ke^{-j3k\omega_0}$.

x(4-t)+y(t-3)\ \leftrightarrow\ a_{-k}e^{-j4k\omega_0}+b_ke^{-j3k\omega_0}.

### Time scaling Here the frequencies themselves change. Compressing time makes every hidden wave rotate faster:

x(\alpha t)=\sum_ka_ke^{jk(\alpha\omega_0)t}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x(\alpha t)\leftrightarrow a_k\ \text{ with new fundamental } \alpha\omega_0\ (\alpha>0).

The coefficient sequence is the same; only the frequency ruler changes. ```fig fs-scaling-views ``` **Practice.** Coefficients of $p(t)=x(4-3t)$: shift left by 4, reverse, then compress by 3.

x(t+4)\leftrightarrow a_ke^{j4k\omega_0},\quad x(4-t)\leftrightarrow a_{-k}e^{-j4k\omega_0},\quad x(4-3t)\leftrightarrow a_{-k}e^{-j4k\omega_0}\ \text{ with }\ \omega_0'=3\omega_0 .

### Differentiation Every little wave gets differentiated: $\frac{d}{dt}e^{jk\omega_0t}=jk\omega_0e^{jk\omega_0t}$, so

\frac{dx}{dt}\leftrightarrow jk\omega_0,a_k .

*Why $jk\omega_0$?* Think of $a_ke^{jk\omega_0t}$ as a point moving on a circle of radius $|a_k|$ at angular speed $k\omega_0$. Its velocity has size $|k\omega_0|\,|a_k|$ (speed = radius × angular speed), and it points **tangent** to the circle, a 90° turn from the position. Multiplying by $j$ is exactly a 90° turn. **Problem.** Coefficients of $\frac{d}{dt}x(4-3t)$: from the practice above, $x(4-3t)\leftrightarrow a_{-k}e^{-j4k\omega_0}$ with $\omega_0'=3\omega_0$. Differentiating multiplies by $jk\omega_0'$:

\frac{d}{dt}x(4-3t)\ \leftrightarrow\ j3k\omega_0,a_{-k}e^{-j4k\omega_0}.

### Drawing derivatives of signals For smooth parts, the derivative is the slope. At a jump, the derivative contains an impulse: a jump of height $A$ at $t_0$ contributes $A\,\delta(t-t_0)$. So

\frac{dx}{dt}=\text{(slope between jumps)}+\text{(impulses at jumps)}.

```fig fs-derivative-sketch ``` ### A detour: the impulse as a value-picker

\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}x[n],\delta[n-a]=x[a],\qquad\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(t),\delta(t-a),dt=x(a).

The impulse is zero everywhere except at $a$, so only one value survives. **But the impulse must be inside the integration window:**

\int_L^R x(t),\delta(t-a),dt=\begin{cases}x(a),&L<a<R\0,&a\notin[L,R]\end{cases}

```fig fs-sift ``` **Practice** with $x(t)=e^t$: - $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^t\delta(t)\,dt=e^0=1$; - $\int_{1}^{\infty}e^t\delta(t)\,dt=0$, because the impulse at $t=0$ is outside the interval; - $\int_{-5}^{5}e^t[\delta(t+1)+2\delta(t-2)]\,dt=e^{-1}+2e^2$. ### Fourier series of an impulse train

x(t)=\sum_{m=-\infty}^{\infty}\delta(t-mT).

Choose the period $-\frac T2<t<\frac T2$, which contains exactly one impulse, $\delta(t)$. By sifting: $$\begin{aligned}&a_k\\[6pt]&= \frac1T\int_{-T/2}^{T/2}\delta(t)e^{-jk\omega_0t}\,dt\\[6pt]&= \frac1Te^{0}\\[6pt]&= \frac1T\quad\text{for every }k. \end{aligned}$$ The coefficient sequence is flat. As a line spectrum in $\omega$, the lines sit at $k\omega_0$: **a train remains a train.** This result is the key to the sampling theorem. ```fig fs-impulse-train ``` ### Checking the differentiation property on the rectangular pulse The periodic rectangular pulse has $a_0=\frac{2T_1}T$ and $a_k=\frac{\sin k\omega_0T_1}{k\pi}$. Its derivative has a $+\delta$ at every rising edge and a $-\delta$ at every falling edge; in one period,

\frac{dx}{dt}=\delta(t+T_1)-\delta(t-T_1).

```fig fs-rect-derivative ``` *Direct calculation* by sifting, calling the coefficients $b_k$: $$\begin{aligned}&b_k\\[6pt]&= \frac1T\int_{-T/2}^{T/2}[\delta(t+T_1)-\delta(t-T_1)]e^{-jk\omega_0t}dt\\[6pt]&= \frac1T\left(e^{jk\omega_0T_1}-e^{-jk\omega_0T_1}\right)\\[6pt]&= \frac{2j}{T}\sin k\omega_0T_1 .\end{aligned}$$ *From the property:* $$\begin{aligned}&jk\omega_0a_k\\[6pt]&= jk\omega_0\dfrac{\sin k\omega_0T_1}{k\pi}\\[6pt]&= \dfrac{j\omega_0}{\pi}\sin k\omega_0T_1\\[6pt]&= \dfrac{2j}T\sin k\omega_0T_1\end{aligned}$$ (using $\omega_0=2\pi/T$). **Perfect match**, and it also gives $b_0=0$, as it must: a derivative of a periodic signal has no average. ### Integration Integration reverses differentiation, so it should divide by the same factor:

\int x(t),dt\ \leftrightarrow\ \frac{a_k}{jk\omega_0},\qquad k\neq0 .

**Warning:** integration cannot recover the constant term, since $\frac{d}{dt}(x+C)=\frac{dx}{dt}$. The coefficient $a_0$ must be found separately (it is the average value). The series of $\int x\,dt$ is periodic only if $a_0=0$ for the original $x$. **Problem: the sawtooth.** $x(t)=t$ for $0\le t<1$, period 1 (so $\omega_0=2\pi$). ```fig fs-sawtooth ``` Between jumps the slope is 1, and at each integer the signal drops by 1: $$\begin{aligned}&y(t)\\[6pt]&= \frac{dx}{dt}\\[6pt]&= 1-\sum_m\delta(t-m).\end{aligned}$$ - The constant 1 has coefficient 1 at $k=0$ only. - The impulse train has coefficient $\frac1T=1$ for every $k$. So $b_0=1-1=0$ and $b_k=-1$ for $k\neq0$. Integrate back: $$\begin{aligned}&a_k\\[6pt]&= \dfrac{b_k}{jk\omega_0}\\[6pt]&= \dfrac{-1}{j2\pi k}\\[6pt]&= \dfrac{j}{2\pi k}\end{aligned}$$ And $a_0$ is the average, $\int_0^1t\,dt=\frac12$:

a_0=\frac12,\qquad a_k=\frac{j}{2\pi k}\ \ (k\neq0).

### Multiplication: convolution returns What about $x(t)y(t)$? Multiply the two series:

x(t)y(t)=\sum_pa_pe^{jp\omega_0t}\sum_qb_qe^{jq\omega_0t}.

With $z=e^{j\omega_0t}$ this is just multiplying two polynomials. A product $a_pb_q\,e^{j(p+q)\omega_0t}$ contributes to harmonic $k$ when $p+q=k$, i.e. $q=k-p$: $$\begin{aligned}&x(t)y(t)\ \leftrightarrow\ c_k\\[6pt]&= \sum_{p=-\infty}^{\infty}a_p\,b_{k-p}\\[6pt]&= (a*b)_k .\end{aligned}$$ *Multiplication in time becomes convolution in frequency.* **Practice.** $x(t)=1+\cos\omega_0t$ has $a_{-1}=\frac12$, $a_0=1$, $a_1=\frac12$. Find the coefficients of $p(t)=x^2(t)$. Convolve $\{\frac12,1,\frac12\}$ with itself: | $k$ | $-2$ | $-1$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | $c_k$ | $\frac14$ | $1$ | $\frac32$ | $1$ | $\frac14$ | ```fig fs-square-signal ``` *Check with trigonometry:* $$\begin{aligned}&(1+\cos\omega_0t)^2\\[6pt]&= 1+2\cos\omega_0t+\cos^2\omega_0t\\[6pt]&= \frac32+2\cos\omega_0t+\frac12\cos2\omega_0t,\end{aligned}$$ so $c_0=\frac32$, $c_{\pm1}=1$, $c_{\pm2}=\frac14$. ✓ ### Parseval's relation

\frac1T\int_T|x(t)|^2dt=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}|a_k|^2 .

The average power of the signal equals the sum of the powers in its harmonics. ### Property table | property | signal | coefficients | |---|---|---| | linearity | $Ax(t)+By(t)$ | $Aa_k+Bb_k$ | | time shift | $x(t-t_0)$ | $a_ke^{-jk\omega_0t_0}$ | | frequency shift | $e^{jM\omega_0t}x(t)$ | $a_{k-M}$ | | time reversal | $x(-t)$ | $a_{-k}$ | | time scaling | $x(\alpha t)$, $\alpha>0$ | $a_k$, with fundamental $\alpha\omega_0$ | | conjugation | $x^*(t)$ | $a_{-k}^*$ | | differentiation | $\frac{dx}{dt}$ | $jk\omega_0a_k$ | | integration | $\int x\,dt$ ($a_0=0$) | $\frac{a_k}{jk\omega_0}$ | | multiplication | $x(t)y(t)$ | $\sum_pa_pb_{k-p}$ | | periodic convolution | $\int_Tx(\tau)y(t-\tau)d\tau$ | $T\,a_kb_k$ | | real signal | $x$ real | $a_{-k}=a_k^*$ | | Parseval | $\frac1T\int_T\lvert x\rvert^2$ | $\sum\lvert a_k\rvert^2$ | ## Exam pointers - For sums of sinusoids, read the coefficients off Euler's formulas; do not integrate. - To decide whether a signal given by its series is real or even: real needs $a_{-k}=a_k^*$, even needs $a_{-k}=a_k$. A series with only $k\ge0$ terms (and some $a_k\ne0$ for $k>0$) is never real. - "Do we need a full cycle?" In general yes (orthogonality); with even or odd symmetry, half a cycle doubled is enough. - Use the derivative trick for piecewise-linear signals: differentiate until you get impulses (whose coefficients are easy by sifting), divide by $jk\omega_0$, and find $a_0$ separately.
